course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 1
unit.description: Follow Native American societies, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the Spanish empire from 1491 to 1607.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
lesson.summary: How maize, aridity, mixed farming, and ocean resources shaped the economies and settlements of Native American societies across North America before 1491.
learningGoals: Identify the regional environments of North America and the ways of life Native societies developed in them.
Explain how the spread of maize cultivation supported irrigation, settlement, and social diversification.
Compare how societies in the Southwest, the Great Basin and Plains, the East, and the Pacific coast met their needs.
lesson.bigIdea: Native societies did not share one way of life. Each adapted to its environment, and those adaptations produced very different economies, settlements, and social structures.
lesson.context: Learning objective B asks how and why native populations interacted with their natural environment. The strongest answers tie a region to its resources and then to the way people organized their lives.

sections.title: Maize cultivation and the Southwest

blocks.text: Maize was first domesticated in what is now Mexico and spread north over centuries into the present-day American Southwest and beyond. Where farmers could water their fields, maize supported denser populations and permanent settlement.

The Hohokam of present-day Arizona dug long irrigation canals to bring river water to desert fields. Ancestral Puebloan peoples built multistory stone and adobe towns, such as the great houses of Chaco Canyon, and their descendants lived in pueblos such as Acoma. Surplus food allowed some people to work as builders, traders, and religious leaders, a change historians call social diversification.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Maize spread north, farmers developed irrigation, harvests grew, and settlements and specialized roles followed. These societies stayed politically separate and never formed a single Southwest empire.

sections.takeaway: Maize and irrigation supported settlement and social diversification in the Southwest, without creating one political system.

sections.title: Mobile societies of the Great Basin and Great Plains
sections.conceptTitle: Mobile societies of the Great Basin and Great Plains

blocks.text: Much of the Great Basin is dry and offers little farmland. Shoshone, Paiute, and Ute families gathered seeds, pine nuts, and roots and hunted small game, moving in small groups with the seasons to follow scarce food.

On the grasslands of the western Great Plains, many peoples hunted bison, which required following the herds. Before horses arrived with Europeans, hunters traveled on foot and used fire and drives to take bison. Some Plains peoples, such as the Mandan, lived in river valleys and farmed as well as hunted, a reminder that one region could hold more than one way of life.

sections.takeaway: Aridity in the Great Basin and bison on the Plains led many societies to largely mobile lifestyles.

sections.title: Mixed economies in the Northeast, Mississippi Valley, and Atlantic seaboard
sections.conceptTitle: Mixed economies in the Northeast, Mississippi Valley, and Atlantic seaboard

blocks.text: In the eastern woodlands and river valleys, many societies combined farming with hunting, fishing, and gathering. Maize, beans, and squash were grown together, and the food they supplied made permanent villages possible.

Mississippian peoples built large mounds and the city of Cahokia, which depended on maize and on trade across a wide region. In the Northeast, the Haudenosaunee lived in villages of longhouses. Algonquian-speaking peoples such as the Lenape and the Secotan of the Roanoke area moved seasonally to fish and hunt but kept fixed villages and fields.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Mixed economies were not the same as mobile ones. These societies farmed and kept permanent villages even when families traveled to hunt or fish.

sections.takeaway: A mix of farming, hunting, and gathering favored permanent villages in the East.

sections.title: The Northwest and California: ocean and river resources
sections.conceptTitle: The Northwest and California: ocean and river resources

blocks.text: Along the Northwest coast, peoples such as the Chinook and the Tlingit relied on salmon, whales, shellfish, and forest products. These reliable resources let them live in settled communities with large plank houses and a rich trade in goods.

In California, many peoples, including the Chumash, supported dense populations without farming, relying on acorns, fish, and sea mammals. Neither region used maize, yet both developed settled and complex societies.

sections.takeaway: Abundant ocean and river resources supported settled communities without agriculture.

connections.title: Environment and the first encounters
connections.body: The way each society used its environment affected how it traded, how it was governed, and how it met Europeans. Topic 1.6 returns to the differing worldviews that came from these ways of life.
connections.transferQuestion: Choose one region and explain how its environment shaped one part of how its people lived.
connections.feedback: A strong answer names a region, a specific resource or condition, and a way of life that resulted from it.
